paragraphs.heading: What they are
paragraphs.text: Maxwell's equations are a set of linked equations that describe how electric charges and currents produce electric and magnetic fields. Combined with the Lorentz force law, they underpin classical electromagnetism and classical optics, as well as electric and magnetic circuits. They give the mathematical model behind power generation, electric motors, wireless communication, lenses and radar.

paragraphs.heading: Gauss's two laws
paragraphs.text: Gauss's law links the electric field to electric charges. The field points away from positive charges and toward negative ones, and the total field flowing out through a closed surface is proportional to the charge inside it. Gauss's law for magnetism says there are no magnetic monopoles: no north or south pole ever exists on its own. Instead, the magnetic field of a material is put down to a dipole, and the net magnetic field flowing out through any closed surface is zero.

paragraphs.heading: Faraday's law
paragraphs.text: Another equation, a version of Faraday's law of induction, ties a magnetic field that changes in time to an electric field. In its integral form, it says the work per unit charge needed to carry a charge around a closed loop equals how fast the magnetic flux through that loop is changing. This electromagnetic induction is how many electric generators work. A spinning bar magnet, for example, makes a changing magnetic field, which in turn produces an electric field in a wire nearby.

paragraphs.heading: Maxwell's addition
paragraphs.text: Another equation starts from Ampère's original law, which ties magnetic fields to electric current. Maxwell added that magnetic fields are also tied to changing electric fields, which he called displacement current. One result is that a changing electric field comes with a rotating magnetic field. Another is that electromagnetic waves can sustain themselves and travel through empty space. Experiments on charges and currents let you predict how fast these waves go, and the answer matches the speed of light, and light is indeed one kind of electromagnetic radiation, as are X-rays and radio waves.

paragraphs.heading: Who wrote them
paragraphs.text: They take their name from James Clerk Maxwell, a physicist and mathematician who published an early form in 1861 and 1862. That work united magnetism, electricity, light and related radiation, which until then had been described separately. In 1861 Maxwell saw the link between electromagnetic waves and light, joining electromagnetism and optics. The modern, most common form is credited to Oliver Heaviside. His vector calculus version became the standard, and it is clearer than Maxwell's original 20 equations written out in x, y and z components.

paragraphs.heading: Versions and limits
paragraphs.text: Two versions are used most. The microscopic equations apply everywhere, but they work with the total charge and current, down to the messy charges and currents inside atoms, which makes them clumsy for everyday calculations. The macroscopic equations bring in two extra fields that describe matter on a large scale without tracking atoms, though they need properties of materials measured by experiment. Since the mid-20th century, physicists have understood that Maxwell's equations are not exact. They are the classical limit of a more precise theory, quantum electrodynamics.
